page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.r5.3xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance based on the KVM hypervisor. It is powered by an Intel Xeon 8163 processor clocked at 2.5 GHz using the x86_64 architecture. The instance configuration features 12 dedicated vCPUs spanning 6 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading, alongside 96.0 GB of system RAM. This provides an 8:1 memory-to-core allocation (8.0 GB per vCPU). The underlying processor includes a 33 MB L3 cache and supports instruction sets such as AVX-512F and AES-NI, though modern matrix extensions such as AMX are not present. No local storage or discrete GPUs are bundled with this instance type, and it operates with a baseline network bandwidth of 4 Gbps.

Benchmark data reflects performance typical of older Intel Xeon architectures. Multi-core operations land consistently in the middle tier, with a PassMark CPU score of 10,083.99, a Geekbench multi-core score of 4,817.0, and a stress-ng multi-core result of 8,830.76. In contrast, single-thread throughput exhibits lower efficiency, evidenced by a Geekbench single-core score of 950.0 and single-threaded gzip compression at 19.12 GB/sec. Uncached large-block memory bandwidth reaches 56.97 GB/sec read and 48.69 GB/sec write. In-memory data handling is moderate, demonstrated by 9.13 million Redis SET operations per second and a PassMark database operations metric of 3,240.47.

From an architectural efficiency standpoint, the ecs.r5.3xlarge favors memory footprint capacity over peak compute density. Because local storage is absent, storage performance relies on attached network volumes over the 4 Gbps baseline link. The instance demonstrates constrained throughput for single-threaded processing and heavier CPU-bound tasks like 7B LLM inference. Its resource allocation is best suited for memory-intensive workloads that do not demand cutting-edge per-core execution speeds, including distributed caching layers, relational database hosting, in-memory analytics, and enterprise enterprise resource planning backends.
